opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was honestly a bit of an adventure. The allocation we had was on Frontier at Oak Ridge, which is a fantastic machine, but it's an AMD system, so you're running on MI250X GPUs with ROCm instead of the NVIDIA stack that almost all of the open-source tooling is built and tested around. A lot of the early work wasn't research at all. It was getting a training pipeline that runs stably and efficiently on that hardware at scale. Things you'd take for granted, like fused attention kernels or communication across many nodes behaving nicely, needed a fair amount of fiddling. We ended up writing a lot of things ourselves and keeping the setup fairly simple, because every extra dependency was another thing that could break.

The bigger challenge was conceptual. At 100 million parameters you can run lots of small experiments, try different recurrence designs, and see what works. But the compute budget meant we basically had one serious shot at the large model. So the question was always, how much do the small-scale results actually tell you about what happens at 3.5 billion parameters with a recurrent-depth architecture? The answer turned out to be: less than you'd hope.

Our first attempts at scale did not work. The model either became unstable or, more frustratingly, learned to just ignore the recurrence. It would train fine in terms of loss, but if you added more iterations at test time, nothing improved, so you'd effectively built an expensive normal transformer. Or the hidden states would collapse and every token would look the same after a few steps. None of that had really shown up at the small scale.

So we went back and made some careful changes: how the input gets re-injected into each recurrent step, the normalization placement, initialization, how we sample the number of iterations during training, and how we truncate backpropagation through the recurrence so memory stays manageable. Those details turned out to be the difference between a model that really uses its depth and one that doesn't. After that, the final run was fairly uneventful. We trained it on around 800 billion tokens, and it actually got better the more it thought at test time.

My takeaway is that with novel architectures, the small-scale ablations are necessary but not sufficient. You need to build in a little slack for something going wrong at scale, and you need to watch the right diagnostics, not just the loss curve, to catch when the model is quietly taking a shortcut.

r001.rationale: It says the compute budget meant they had “basically one serious shot” at the large model.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a 512-node allocation or a 128-node workload limit.

r003.rationale: It does not mention restricting communication to 64-megabyte packets or link that to interconnect stability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was really a story of constraints shaping the research. We had an allocation on Frontier at Oak Ridge, which is an AMD machine, and that's already the first practical challenge: a lot of the tooling that people take for granted in the NVIDIA ecosystem just isn't there, or it's there but it's a few months behind. So we spent a nontrivial amount of time just getting a stable training stack, making sure the communication collectives behaved the way we expected, dealing with nodes that would go down in the middle of a run. On a machine like that you don't get to pick your hardware; you get the allocation, you get the time window, and you have to make it work.

The second thing is that at 100 million parameters you can be sloppy. You can try twenty variants of the architecture in a week and let the results tell you what to do. At 3.5 billion you don't have that luxury. Each run is expensive enough that you really only get a handful of real attempts, and we weren't a big industry lab with the budget to burn a few of those on debugging. So a lot of our strategy was to front-load everything at small scale: figure out the recurrence depth, the normalization scheme, the initialization, the learning rate schedule, all at sizes where failures are cheap, and then try to be very disciplined about what we change when we scale up.

And the honest answer is that it still didn't fully transfer. Recurrent models in particular have this property that things that look fine at small scale can become unstable when you go deeper and wider, because you're iterating the same block many times and small issues compound. We had a couple of runs that diverged, and because the compute window was fixed, every one of those cost us real training steps we never got back. So the final model is trained on fewer tokens than we would have liked, and that's a direct consequence of the allocation, not of the design.

The last piece is just the mindset of it. When you have a fixed budget, you stop optimizing for "the best possible model" and start optimizing for "the model that is most likely to actually finish and tell us something." That meant being conservative in some places where a larger lab might have been aggressive, and it meant accepting that the paper would be about the idea and about whether the approach is viable, rather than about topping a leaderboard. I think that's a reasonable trade, and frankly it's the trade most academic groups have to make if they want to do pretraining research at all.

r001.rationale: The response says the limited allocation made each large run expensive, allowing only “a handful of real attempts,” which ties the near one-shot scaling process to limited compute.

r002.rationale: It mentions Frontier and practical cluster constraints but does not identify a 512-node allocation or a 128-node intended limit.

r003.rationale: It mentions communication collectives, but not restricting data-parallel communication to exactly 64-megabyte packets or how that stabilized training on the interconnect.

astra-6.text:
The big challenge is that scaling the model also changes how you have to run the experiments. At 100 million parameters, you can iterate quickly. At 3.5 billion, every experiment takes a much larger fraction of your compute budget, so you have to be more selective about what you test.

The strategy is to resolve as many questions as possible at the smaller scale, then use intermediate runs to check which choices transfer. And you have to treat the systems side as part of the research: how you distribute the model, how much memory you need for optimizer states and activations, and whether communication between devices is eating up the benefit of having more devices.

With a fixed supercomputer allocation, the important quantity is useful training progress within the time you have. That means budgeting for debugging and checkpointing, as well as the final run. You want to reach the larger scale with a setup you understand well enough that you’re spending the allocation learning something, rather than discovering basic infrastructure problems.

r001.rationale: The response says the larger run uses a much larger share of a fixed compute budget, but does not communicate that scaling up was effectively a one-shot attempt.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a 512-node allocation or a 128-node limit for deep learning workloads.

r003.rationale: It discusses device communication generally, but does not identify restricting data-parallel communication to exactly 64-megabyte packets or say that this stabilized training.

sol-6.1.text:
The big challenge was that we had a fixed compute allocation, so we couldn’t simply scale up every experiment. At 100 million parameters, you can try things, see what breaks, and iterate relatively quickly. At 3.5 billion, a mistake becomes much more expensive.

So we used the smaller models to work through as many of the training decisions as possible before committing to the larger run. And then there’s the systems side: making sure the model fits in memory, that computation is distributed efficiently, and that you can save and resume reliably. Having access to a supercomputer is only useful if you can actually keep the hardware busy.

It becomes a balancing act between spending compute to reduce uncertainty and preserving enough compute to train the final model. You want to enter that large run with a configuration you understand, while accepting that some things only become apparent at scale.

r001.rationale: The response connects the fixed compute allocation to costly large-model experiments, but does not clearly communicate that the limited allocation made scaling up effectively a one-shot attempt.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the 512-node allocation or the cluster’s 128-node limit for deep-learning workloads.

r003.rationale: It discusses distributed efficiency generally, but does not identify 64-megabyte communication packets or their role in stabilizing training on the interconnect.
